name: TNY268PN
title: TinySwitch-II TNY263-268 off-line switcher with integrated 700 V MOSFET
summary: A family of six off-line switchers, TNY263 to TNY268, each putting a 700 V power MOSFET and its controller in one 8-lead package with pin 6 removed. The chip powers itself from its own DRAIN pin, so a flyback built on it needs no bias winding, and it regulates by simple ON/OFF control: each 132 kHz cycle either runs to the current limit or is skipped, set by current drawn out of EN/UV, usually by an optocoupler. The same pin takes an optional resistor from the DC bus for line undervoltage lockout, and the part adds frequency jitter, auto-restart, a light-load current limit state machine and thermal shutdown. The family is marked not recommended for new designs.

The figures assume: a minimum DC input of 90 V or more at 85 VAC, or 240 V or more at 230 VAC or at 115 VAC with a doubler (bulk capacitance of 3 µF/W on universal input, or 1 µF/W at 230 VAC or doubled 115 VAC); a 5 V secondary with a Schottky rectifier; efficiency of 77% (TNY267, TNY268), 75% (TNY265, TNY266) and 73% (TNY263, TNY264); and the SOURCE pins soldered to enough copper to hold the die at or below 100 °C.

The power reached in a given design also depends on the enclosure, the transformer core and whether it runs continuous or discontinuous, efficiency, the lowest specified input voltage, input storage capacitance, output voltage and the output diode's forward drop.

circuits.title: Typical standby application
circuits.description: A flyback around the part. A high-voltage DC bus feeds the primary; an RC network with a series diode clamps the DRAIN spike at turn-off. The secondary is rectified and smoothed into the DC output. A Zener in series with the optocoupler LED sets the output: once the output passes the Zener plus LED drop, the phototransistor pulls EN/UV down to the primary return and cycles are skipped. A resistor across the LED biases the Zener. The resistor from the bus to EN/UV is optional and sets the line undervoltage level. BP has only its capacitor.

A, K the LED; C, E the phototransistor

circuits.title: 2.5 W constant voltage, constant current charger, 85-265 VAC
circuits.description: A TNY264 cell-phone charger giving 5 V at 0.5 A from a universal AC input. A fusible resistor and a four-diode bridge feed two 3.3 µF bulk capacitors, with L1 (damped by R1) between their returns as a pi filter. D6, R2 and C3 clamp the leakage spike at DRAIN. A shield winding in T1 and the 680 pF Y1 capacitor C8 keep conducted EMI in limits with the output earthed. The secondary is rectified by the Schottky D5 into C5, followed by an L2-C6 filter. In voltage mode the output sits at the optocoupler LED drop (about 1 V) plus VR1's 3.9 V, R8 keeping VR1 near its test current. In current mode, the drop across the sense resistor R4 turns Q1 on, and Q1 drives the LED itself; R6 keeps enough voltage for the loop to work with the output shorted, and R7 and R9 limit the current Q1 can pull through VR1 then.

circuits.title: 10 W standby supply
circuits.description: A standby supply with two outputs from a TNY266P, running on a 140-375 VDC bus (230 VAC, or 100/115 VAC with a doubler): an isolated +5 V at 2 A and a +12 V, 20 mA output tied to the primary for the main converter's controller. TNY266P gives 10.24 W of continuous output at 75% or better efficiency. C1 decouples the bus, needed only when the bulk capacitors of the main supply are far away. R1, C5 and D1 clamp the DRAIN. R2 and R3, 2 MΩ together, sense the bus so the part starts above about 200 VDC and then keeps running down to 140 VDC, and stays off without glitches when the AC goes away. The bias winding, D2 and C2 make the 12 V rail, which also feeds BP through R4 (10 kΩ, about 600 µA, a little more than the part consumes), so the internal drain current source stays idle; the surplus goes into the 6.3 V clamp. D3 and C6 rectify the secondary, and L1 with C8 filter switching noise. VR1 and the optocoupler sense the 5 V output; R5 holds VR1 at its test current and R6 centres the output at 5 V.

operation.text: The TNY263-268 family is not recommended for new designs.

One die holds the 700 V power MOSFET, an oscillator, the enable circuit with its sense and logic, the current limit state machine, a 5.8 V regulator, a BYPASS undervoltage circuit, thermal shutdown, the current limit comparator with leading edge blanking, and circuits for line undervoltage sensing, auto-restart and frequency jitter.

The oscillator runs at 132 kHz on average and produces the DCMAX signal and a clock that marks the start of each cycle. Its frequency is swept by about 8 kHz peak to peak (128 to 136 kHz) at a 1 kHz rate, lowering both quasi-peak and average EMI. The jitter is seen on a scope triggered on the falling DRAIN edge.

EN/UV is a low-impedance source follower at 1.0 V whose current is limited to 240 µA. Drawing more than that out of the pin gives a disable level. The enable output is sampled on the rising clock edge at the start of each cycle: high turns the MOSFET on for that cycle, low leaves it off, and changes later in the cycle are ignored. An enabled cycle always completes, ending when the drain current reaches the current limit or DCMAX is reached. Output ripple is therefore set by the output capacitor, the energy per cycle and the feedback delay. Except near no load, the follower holds EN/UV not far below 1.0 V when disabled, which speeds the optocoupler's response. The control needs no loop compensation and responds faster than PWM control.

The clock runs continuously, and from the sequence of EN/UV samples over many cycles the state machine picks the current limit. Near full load nearly every cycle conducts; slightly lower, some cycles are skipped; at medium loads cycles are skipped and the current limit is lowered; at very light loads it is lowered further and only a few cycles occur. Lowering the limit in steps keeps the effective switching frequency above the audio band and reduces flux density in the transformer, so ordinary dip-varnished transformers need no gluing.

The EN/UV signal comes from the secondary, high while the output is below its reference. Usually an optocoupler's collector goes to EN/UV and its emitter to SOURCE, its LED in series with a Zener across the output: once the output exceeds the LED drop plus the Zener voltage, the LED conducts and pulls EN/UV low. A TL431 can replace the Zener for better accuracy. With a Zener, regulation is typically within ± 6% over 0 °C to 50 °C, since the part keeps the LED current range narrow.

While the MOSFET is off, the regulator charges the BYPASS capacitor to 5.8 V from the DRAIN voltage; while it is on, the chip runs from the energy in that capacitor. A 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor is enough for both decoupling and storage. When current is fed into BP through an outside resistor, a shunt clamps the pin at 6.3 V; powering the chip this way from a bias winding (at least 750 µA recommended) cuts no-load consumption to about 50 mW and removes the draw from DRAIN.
The MOSFET is disabled when BP falls below 4.8 V, and it is enabled again only once BP has risen back to 5.8 V.
The MOSFET is disabled when the die passes typically 135 °C and stays off until the die has cooled by 70 °C. The wide hysteresis keeps a lasting fault from overheating the board.

operation.topic: Current limit and leading edge blanking
operation.text: The MOSFET turns off for the rest of a cycle once its current passes ILIMIT. For a short time tLEB after turn-on the comparator is blanked, so spikes from capacitance and secondary rectifier reverse recovery do not end the pulse early. Limiting each cycle at a fixed current rejects line ripple and keeps delivered power fairly constant against input voltage.

An oscillator-clocked counter is reset each time EN/UV is pulled low. If it is not pulled low for 50 ms (an overload, short circuit or open loop), switching is normally disabled for 850 ms, and enabling and disabling alternate until the fault clears. The effective on-time is about 6%, which keeps short-circuit output current below full load current, so the output diode need not be oversized and no second optocoupler and Zener are needed for open-loop protection. During a line undervoltage the counter stops and the off time lasts until the undervoltage ends.

A resistor from the DC bus to EN/UV monitors the line. At power-up, or after an auto-restart off period, switching starts only once more than 49 µA flows into the pin; at power-up BP is held at 4.8 V until then, rising to 5.8 V afterwards. With less than about 2 µA into the pin the function is disabled.

BP needs only 0.1 µF, which charges in typically 0.6 ms, and the fast ON/OFF loop gives no output overshoot. With a 2 MΩ resistor from the positive DC input to EN/UV, switching waits until the bus exceeds 100 V. At power-down with the resistor fitted, the MOSFET keeps switching for 50 ms after the output falls out of regulation and then stays off without glitches, because the undervoltage function blocks a restart at low line; this matters in standby supplies whose bulk capacitors discharge slowly.

Because the chip draws its power from DRAIN, a nominal design needs no bias winding. In chargers the output can fall close to 0 V while power is still delivered, which otherwise calls for a forward-bias winding. Constant voltage, constant current outputs that must work down to zero volts are simpler for the same reason.

Cell-phone chargers, PC and TV standby supplies, AC adapters, motor and appliance control, and ISDN or DSL network termination. At 132 kHz an EE13 or EF12.6 core is usable, and with the jitter one inductor (or, below 3 W where lower efficiency is acceptable, two small resistors) with two input capacitors can form the input EMI filter. Removing pin 6 gives a large creepage distance at DRAIN for dusty or fan-cooled supplies.
Identical supplies can run at different frequencies at the same line and load, so measurements are made with the part at its maximum frequency and at both low and high line.

The DRAIN peak at turn-off is clamped by an RCD network, a Zener and diode (200 V) across the primary, or a single 550 V Zener from DRAIN to SOURCE, with short paths from the clamp to the transformer and the part.
The voltage rating of the undervoltage resistors matters: 1/4 W resistors are typically rated 200 V continuous, 1/2 W resistors 400 V.

The BYPASS capacitor and input filter capacitor return to a single point at SOURCE. The primary loop through the input filter capacitor, the transformer primary and the part is kept as small as possible, as is the loop through the secondary winding, output diode and output filter capacitor. Copper under the part is both the single-point ground and the heatsink and is made as large as possible, as is copper at the output diode's terminals. A UV resistor sits as close to EN/UV as it can. The optocoupler connects to EN/UV and SOURCE by the shortest path; the EN/UV trace is under 12.7 mm (0.5 in.) and at least 5.1 mm (0.2 in.) from DRAIN. The Y capacitor goes from the primary bulk capacitor's positive rail straight to the secondary common/return terminal. Narrowed traces at the input and output filter capacitors force ripple current through them and cut heat flow into them. The output common/return terminal connects by a short low-impedance path to the secondary winding pin, not to the Y capacitor's connection.
No-clean flux is not recommended.
